name: Age of Discovery 1492
description: Granada has fallen, and Christopher Columbus is begging the courts of Europe for ships. Two worlds are about to collide — chart unknown coasts and claim them, or hold your empire against strangers from over the sea. (Map borders approximate realms onto modern outlines.)

ESP.name: Castile & Aragon
ESP.note: Isabella and Ferdinand have taken Granada and expelled the last emirate. A Genoese sailor waits at court with a mad westward scheme.

PRT.name: Kingdom of Portugal
PRT.note: John II's captains have rounded the Cape of Good Hope; the sea road to India is almost open, and Lisbon guards its charts like state secrets.

FRA.name: Kingdom of France
FRA.note: Charles VIII, young and hungry for glory, eyes the crowns of Naples and a crusade beyond.

GBR.name: Kingdom of England
GBR.note: Henry VII Tudor counts his coins and marries off his children, rebuilding a realm exhausted by the Wars of the Roses.

ITA.name: Papal States
ITA.note: Innocent VIII is dying; the conclave that follows may sell the Fisherman's Ring to a Borgia.

TUR.name: Ottoman Empire
TUR.note: Bayezid II consolidates Mehmed's conquests, welcomes Iberia's expelled Jews, and dominates the eastern Mediterranean.

MEX.name: Aztec Triple Alliance
MEX.note: Ahuitzotl's armies carry obsidian and tribute demands across Mesoamerica. Of Europe, nothing is known.

PER.name: Inca Empire
PER.note: The Sapa Inca rules the largest empire in the Americas through roads, storehouses, and knotted cords. Of Europe, nothing is known.

CHN.name: Ming China
CHN.note: The Hongzhi Emperor governs frugally and well. The treasure fleets are burned; the sea is officially closed.

world.simulationRules: Age of sail: ocean crossings take months and ships vanish in storms. Unmapped coasts may be charted and claimed at country granularity once expeditions actually reach them — no instant knowledge of distant continents. First contact between hemispheres is world-changing: disease devastates populations without immunity, and news travels at the speed of a caravel. Legitimacy flows from crowns, faith, and papal arbitration (a Tordesillas-style division of the unknown world is possible). The Aztec and Inca courts know nothing of Europe until contact, and vice versa.
